title: How an AI agent is tested before and after it ships
subtitle: Offline simulations and calibrated judges gate every change; live traces feed failures back into prompts and test sets.
hook: A judge that gates nothing is useless: here every score decides whether a change ships.

sources.title: Building Closed-Loop Evals for a Multimodal Agent at Scale
sources.speaker: Soumya Gupta & Jai Chopra

nodes.label: Agent engineer
nodes.detail: Edits the system prompt, tools, context or agent graph of Lyft's customer support agent. Like an ML model, the agent must pass offline evals before it reaches users.
nodes.tradeoff: Lyft's rule: live users are never the test data for an agent.

nodes.label: Golden dataset
nodes.detail: Built from sampled production conversations, plus mutated copies that cover golden paths and edge cases. Domain experts label traces in annotation queues, and labeled traces join the dataset.
nodes.tradeoff: Asking an LLM for 50 test queries gives data that looks nothing like production, a key gotcha for Lyft.

nodes.label: Eval harness
nodes.detail: A config-driven harness: tasks, datasets, personas, model adapters and evaluators are defined once in YAML, so analysts can add cases too. It runs thousands of examples in parallel.
nodes.tradeoff: Lyft's first simulations were scattered notebook scripts that were not repeatable; a standard harness is their next investment.

nodes.label: User simulator
nodes.detail: Inspired by τ-bench, an LLM plays the customer in full multi-turn chats, given an intent, account state and a persona such as refund seeker or AI skeptic. Lyft fine-tuned it on real user messages.
nodes.tradeoff: A polite frontier model as the user gave a 90%+ pass rate; realistic users lowered scores, which is what you want.

nodes.label: LLM judge
nodes.detail: Binary pass/fail rubrics written with domain experts, plus code assertions, such as checking the agent granted a concession when it should. The judge is treated as a classifier: precision and recall against about 100 hand-labeled examples.
nodes.tradeoff: Pre-built DeepEval scores like helpfulness were a baseline but not actionable, so Lyft moved to task-specific binary judges.

nodes.label: Launch gate
nodes.detail: A change ships only if offline evals meet the launch criteria. Lyft already runs the suite as a pre-commit hook, and is building a regression suite into CI/CD.
nodes.tradeoff: 84% versus 88% on 50 traces may be noise; add confidence intervals before a shipping decision.

nodes.label: Live agent
nodes.detail: Lyft's customer support agent is a multi-agent system built with LangGraph, answering riders and drivers in production.
nodes.tradeoff: Real users are impatient and terse, which makes the agent much harder to evaluate than polite simulated users.

nodes.label: Traces and graders
nodes.detail: Each trace records the full graph run: which nodes ran, what the LLM saw, tool calls, tokens and latency per call. Online graders score live conversations, and experts review failures.
nodes.tradeoff: Everything depends on traces: without them there is no error analysis, no labels, and no way to check the judge.

nodes.label: Prompt optimizer
nodes.detail: Uber samples production on a schedule and has humans label it. A diagnoser finds which agent disagrees with the labels; reflect and synthesize agents then rewrite that agent's config.
nodes.tradeoff: The new config ships only if it passes the golden set; no human in the loop, but guardrails are watched and rollback is quick.

flow.text: An engineer edits the support agent's system prompt.
The harness replays thousands of test cases from config, in parallel.
A fine-tuned user model plays impatient customers across multi-turn chats.
Binary rubric judges and code checks grade every conversation.
The change ships only if the launch criteria still pass.
The LangGraph agent now answers real users.
Every run is traced; graders and experts flag the failures.
A diagnoser rewrites the failing prompt and re-tests it on the golden set.

takeaways.text: An LLM judge score that gates nothing is useless; tie every judge to a launch decision.
Lyft's polite simulated users scored 90%+; fine-tuning on real messages made evals harder and truer.
Uber's loop samples production, labels it, auto-tunes prompts, and ships only after passing the golden set.
